term: Text to speech in digital television
definition: Text to speech in digital television refers to digital television products that use speech synthesis (computer-generated speech that “talks” to the end user) to enable access to blind or partially sighted people.
details: By combining a digital television (a television, set-top box, personal video recorder, or other type of receiver) with a speech synthesis engine, blind and partially sighted people are able to access information that is normally displayed visually in order to operate the menus and electronic program guides of the receiver.

explainer.lead: Speech synthesis built into TVs and receivers so that blind and partially sighted users can hear information other viewers read on screen. It matters because the menus and program guides needed to operate the equipment would otherwise be inaccessible.

tiers.eli5: Your TV reads its own menus out loud, so if you can't see the screen, you can still find channels and settings by listening.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers add a speech engine to a receiver so it speaks menu and electronic program guide items as the user navigates. Pitfall: on-screen interfaces are designed visually, so the spoken layer must cover every menu state without gaps.
tiers.paperLevel: Defined by function: a digital television product (television, set-top box, personal video recorder, or other receiver) combined with a speech synthesis engine that provides spoken access to information normally displayed visually.

explainer.example: A partially sighted viewer opens the electronic program guide on a set-top box and the receiver speaks the highlighted program's title and time instead of only showing it.
